idiom_name: hand-rolled operation id (getrandom(2)) + deduplication by SQLite UPSERT ON CONFLICT
implementation_notes: C has no HTTP client and no retry facility in the standard library, so every part of the pattern is hand-written: draw 16 bytes from getrandom(2) (or /dev/urandom) before the first attempt, render a canonical UUIDv4 string, keep it in the pending-work record, and let the retry loop reuse that same value on every attempt. Detection is delegated to the store rather than to application logic: a UNIQUE index on the key with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(key) DO NOTHING (or an equivalent conditional insert) makes exactly one attempt the winner, and the affected-row count tells the loser that the operation already ran. Nothing replaces the classic structure here; the one honest simplification is to make the effect itself idempotent - an upsert keyed on a business identifier instead of a key table.
pitfalls: The key must be generated and persisted (fsync the pending-work record) before the first attempt; a key that exists only in a stack buffer is lost on crash and the replay becomes a second charge.
getrandom(2) blocks until the entropy pool is initialised unless GRND_NONBLOCK is passed, so seed once at start-up rather than drawing inside the retry loop.
UPSERT arbitrates only when a real UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint exists; without it the second INSERT succeeds and the deduplication silently disappears.
